issues.description: The manuscript says it uses social learning theory but then describes and tests a stressor-emotion process. Social learning theory concerns observational learning/modeling, whereas the hypothesized mediation is based on stress appraisal, negative affect, fatigue, and counterproductive behavior. This theoretical inconsistency weakens the conceptual rationale for the model and makes it unclear which theory generates the hypotheses.
issues.quote: “To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).”

issues.description: The study treats patients and families as “customers,” but nurse-patient relationships differ substantially from conventional customer-service relationships because they involve clinical vulnerability, ethical duties of care, legal obligations, health literacy asymmetries, family involvement, and clinical decision authority. This affects construct validity and limits generalization to service work broadly.
issues.quote: “We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship.”

issues.description: Experienced incivility is defined as coming from patients and families/friends, enacted incivility is toward patients and families/friends, but negative emotions are measured only toward patients. The mediational chain therefore mixes sources and targets: incivility from a family member may be modeled as producing emotions toward patients and then incivility toward patients/families. This ambiguity weakens interpretation of the mechanism.
issues.quote: “The incivility examined is therefore incivility from patients and their families (experienced incivility) and incivility towards patients and their families (enacted incivility).”

issues.description: Recruitment relied on local flyers, personal networks, social media, online forums, and voluntary opt-in. This is a nonprobability, self-selected sample that may overrepresent nurses interested in incivility, nurses with strong negative experiences, or individuals connected to the researchers. Selection bias threatens external validity and may inflate associations among study variables.
issues.quote: “Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies. First, we dropped off recruitment flyers with the study information at three hospitals local to the research team… Second, we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks… Finally, we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts…”

issues.subcategory: unknown sampling frame and response rate
issues.description: The manuscript cannot report the eligible population, denominator contacted, or response rate. Without a sampling frame or response information, nonresponse bias cannot be evaluated and generalizability is unclear.
issues.quote: “Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown…”

issues.description: The recruitment materials reportedly required full-time nurses in high-stakes/critical care settings, but the final sample is described as including part-time nurses. This inconsistency raises concerns about whether the prespecified population was actually sampled and whether eligibility criteria were enforced.
issues.quote: “Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided…”

issues.description: Eligibility appears to have been verified only by emphasizing the nursing focus and asking participants to self-report eligibility. Given open online recruitment through social media and QR codes, this is insufficient to ensure that respondents were nurses working in the intended settings, increasing risk of ineligible or fraudulent participation.
issues.quote: “To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.”

issues.description: The reported participant counts do not reconcile. The manuscript states that 468 responded at Time 1 and 450 at Time 4, which implies 18 fewer respondents, but later says 16 were excluded for missing time points. It also states that 78 were excluded for poor data quality, but the listed reasons account for only 57 exclusions. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the analytic sample and data-cleaning process.
issues.quote: “Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample… (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1). This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.”

issues.description: The final sample is reported as N = 372, but the main tables report N = 321 and the moderation analyses report N = 244. The manuscript does not clearly explain why 51 participants are omitted from the main analyses or why the analytic sample differs across models. This affects reproducibility and may indicate unreported missing-data decisions.
issues.quote: “This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.”

issues.subcategory: complete-case analysis and potential attrition bias
issues.description: The study excluded anyone who missed a wave rather than using available longitudinal data through FIML, multiple imputation, or mixed models. Complete-case analysis can bias estimates if missingness is related to incivility, fatigue, workload, shift patterns, or other study variables. The exclusion also wastes information from partially completed longitudinal responses.
issues.quote: “Only participants who completed all four surveys… were included in the final sample.”

issues.description: The comparison of dropouts to completers is informal and uses a very weak criterion—being within one standard deviation of the final sample mean. No statistical tests, standardized differences, or comparisons for the much larger data-quality exclusions are reported. This does not adequately establish that excluded participants were comparable to retained participants.
issues.quote: “Participants who responded only to the T1 survey reported similar demographic information compared to those who completed all four time periods and had scale values on the key study constructs within one standard deviation of the means for the final sample…”

issues.description: Participants who missed one survey were not invited to subsequent waves. This creates monotone attrition by design and may disproportionately exclude nurses with high workload, fatigue, or stress—the very phenomena under study.
issues.quote: “Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys…”

issues.description: Patient acuity, a central moderator, is measured with a single newly created subjective percentage item rather than an objective acuity score or validated scale. Because acuity systems vary by unit and specialty, respondents’ interpretations are unlikely to be comparable. This threatens construct validity of the moderator.
issues.quote: “we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were ‘severe.’”

issues.description: The measure asks nurses across diverse units to use their own department’s acuity scale, while examples include very different instruments. A percentage classified as “severe” under one system may not be equivalent to the same percentage under another, creating measurement non-equivalence across respondents.
issues.quote: “Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools.”

issues.subcategory: high missingness and invalid responses on moderator
issues.description: The patient acuity item generated substantial missing or invalid data, including responses outside the expected numerical range. This indicates that respondents may not have understood or been able to complete the item reliably. Because moderation depends on this variable, the validity and power of the moderation findings are compromised.
issues.quote: “Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response).”

issues.subcategory: large unexplained sample reduction for moderation
issues.description: The moderation analysis uses N = 244, far below the reported final N = 372 and the main table N = 321. The reduction is attributed to moderator missingness, but no missing-data mechanism analysis or correction is reported. If acuity missingness is related to unit type, workload, distress, or survey comprehension, the moderation results may be biased.
issues.quote: “Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.”

issues.description: The acuity moderator is a percentage of severe patients, but workload burden depends on both proportion and number of patients. A nurse with 1 severe patient out of 1 and a nurse with 10 severe patients out of 10 both score 100%, despite very different workloads. The authors acknowledge not collecting patient counts, which undermines interpretation of acuity as workload demand.
issues.quote: “we did not ask them to report on the specific assessment used, number of patients seen in that week, or the number of patients that were actually classified as severe within their assessment tool.”

issues.subcategory: shortened scales selected by factor loadings
issues.description: The authors shortened scales by selecting the highest-loading items. This can narrow the construct domain, inflate reliability, and omit theoretically important facets, especially after adapting the scale to a new patient/family context and weekly time frame.
issues.quote: “For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability…”

issues.subcategory: inflated validation evidence for shortened scales
issues.description: Part-whole correlations between shortened and full scales are not strong evidence of validity because the shortened items are included in the full scale, mechanically inflating the correlation. This is especially problematic because the adapted enacted and experienced incivility scales are central to the study.
issues.quote: “assessed part-whole correlations between the full scales and shortened versions during pilot testing (r (48) = .91, p < .001 for experienced patient incivility and r (48) = .93, p <.001for enacted patient incivility)”

issues.subcategory: questionable item validity in healthcare context
issues.description: Some incivility items may not represent incivility in clinical care. Patients or family members questioning a nurse’s judgment can be legitimate advocacy, confusion, fear, or informed decision-making rather than rude or deviant behavior. Misclassifying legitimate clinical interactions as incivility may bias results, especially when patient acuity is high.
issues.quote: “Doubted your judgment on a matter over which you had responsibility”

issues.description: The enacted-incivility scale mirrors the experienced-incivility items, but some items are awkward or clinically ambiguous when applied to patients/families. For example, doubting a patient’s or family member’s judgment may reflect appropriate clinical guidance rather than incivility. This threatens construct validity of the outcome.
issues.quote: “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility”

issues.subcategory: common item wording and criterion contamination
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility are measured with nearly identical item content and the same self-report format. This increases shared method variance and semantic overlap, making the observed relationship between experienced and enacted incivility partly a measurement artifact.
issues.quote: “The item content for these four items was similar to the four items used in the customer incivility scale, with changes to the instructions that prompted participants to respond about how they behaved towards their patients…”

issues.description: The primary behavioral outcome is self-reported mistreatment of patients/families. Such behavior is socially undesirable and may be underreported, distorted by self-presentation, or affected by respondents’ negative affect. No patient, peer, supervisor, or observational corroboration is used.
issues.quote: “Participants were asked, ‘Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?’”

issues.subcategory: weekly measurement of chronic compassion fatigue
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is described as progressive and cumulative, but it is measured with a past-week frequency frame. A weekly state-like assessment may not validly capture the chronic construct of compassion fatigue, and the manuscript does not establish that the adapted time frame has been validated.
issues.quote: “For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.”

issues.subcategory: aggregate compassion fatigue despite multidimensional definition
issues.description: The manuscript defines compassion fatigue as having burnout and secondary trauma components and states that either component can qualify as compassion fatigue, yet it appears to use one aggregate 13-item score. This may obscure different mechanisms and misrepresent the construct, because burnout-like fatigue and secondary traumatic stress may have different antecedents and consequences.
issues.quote: “Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously).”

issues.description: The quantitative pilot used only 50 MTurk-recruited nurses, and eligibility verification for this pilot is not described. Such a small and potentially unverified pilot is insufficient to validate adapted shortened scales and a newly created acuity item for high-stakes nursing contexts.
issues.quote: “The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk.”

issues.description: The study uses repeated measures over four waves and adapted shortened scales, but reports only a general CFA. It does not test whether measurement structure, loadings, thresholds/intercepts, or residuals are invariant across time. Without longitudinal invariance, apparent changes or lagged associations may reflect measurement differences across waves.
issues.quote: “First, we assessed our hypothesized four-factor model absent of the temporal control measures.”

issues.description: The CFA is reported only for the hypothesized model, with no detailed alternative model statistics, no factor correlations, and no discriminant validity indices. Given extremely high correlations among constructs, CFA fit alone is insufficient to show that incivility, negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility are empirically distinct.
issues.quote: “The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.”

issues.description: Several correlations among theoretically distinct constructs are extremely high, including correlations around .85-.94. Such values raise serious concerns about discriminant validity, common method bias, response style, or construct redundancy. The mediational interpretation is questionable if the variables are not empirically separable.

The longitudinal mediation does not appear to control for prior levels of the mediator or outcome variables, such as T1/T2 negative emotions, T1/T2 compassion fatigue, or prior enacted incivility. Without autoregressive controls, lagged coefficients may reflect stable between-person differences, negative affectivity, unit climate, or preexisting compassion fatigue rather than change over time.
issues.quote: “We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).”

issues.description: Although data were collected repeatedly, the analysis uses variables from selected waves rather than modeling within-person change or separating within-person from between-person effects. Therefore, findings may indicate that nurses who generally perceive more incivility also generally report more negative emotions and fatigue, not that incivility exposure produces later changes.
issues.quote: “The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing (see Figure 1 for information what measurement period each variable in the model was taken from).”

issues.description: The manuscript frames the study as examining chronic or cumulative weekly exposure, but the main hypotheses use a single week of incivility predicting later variables. The analysis does not compute cumulative exposure, repeated exposure trajectories, or within-person accumulation across four weeks.
issues.quote: “we propose that it is not only important to examine events-based reactions to incivility from a single person… but also how cumulative weekly exposure to incivility across customers and workdays can influence employee wellbeing and behaviors.”

issues.description: The final mediator, compassion fatigue, and outcome, enacted incivility, are both measured at Time 4. This prevents establishing temporal precedence for the last step of the serial mediation. The claim that compassion fatigue leads to enacted incivility is not supported by a same-wave association.

issues.subcategory: serial indirect effect calculation unclear or incorrectly described
issues.description: For a serial mediation from incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility, the indirect effect should involve the product of all component paths in the sequence. The manuscript states that the effect was estimated by multiplying only the “first and last stages” and labels this as a × d, which is unclear and potentially incorrect. This ambiguity impairs reproducibility of the central hypothesis test.
issues.quote: “Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).”

issues.description: The same indirect effect is reported with different standard errors in the text and table. The text reports SE = .04, whereas Table 2 reports SE = .02. This discrepancy affects the p-value and confidence in the reported significance of Hypothesis 4.
issues.quote: “Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]).”

issues.subcategory: no total effect reported for mediation
issues.description: The manuscript emphasizes an indirect relationship from experienced incivility to enacted incivility, but the direct path shown in the mediation table is negative and nonsignificant after mediators. The total effect is not reported. Without the total effect and with a nonsignificant/negative direct effect, claims that experienced incivility is related to increased enacted incivility require more careful qualification.

The manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as “effect,” “drives,” and “causal inferences,” but the design is observational, self-report, nonrandomized, and vulnerable to confounding and reverse causality. Temporal separation alone does not establish causation.
issues.quote: “This method also supports a lower likelihood of third variable effects… and allows for stronger causal inferences by modeling the longitudinal effects of predictors across multiple points in time.”

issues.description: The models appear to control primarily for work hours, while omitting plausible confounders such as negative affectivity, baseline burnout, unit type, shift type, patient ratios, hospital/unit civility climate, coworker/supervisor incivility, tenure, age, and gender. Omitted variables could explain both perceived incivility and later emotions/fatigue/enacted incivility.

Participants were recruited from multiple hospitals and likely nested within units/departments, but the analyses do not account for clustering. Shared unit climate, leadership, patient population, and workload could induce nonindependence and bias standard errors and effect estimates.
issues.quote: “Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S.”

issues.description: The interaction between experienced incivility and patient acuity uses two Time 2 self-reported variables. Because both are measured concurrently and subjectively, the interaction may reflect common negative appraisal or current affect rather than acuity objectively exacerbating the effect of incivility.
issues.quote: “Results revealed that the Time 2 experienced incivility × Time 2 perceived patient acuity interaction term was significant…”

issues.subcategory: moderated mediation not supported but interpreted broadly
issues.description: The supplemental moderated mediation analysis found that conditional indirect effects and the index of moderated mediation were nonsignificant, yet later practical interpretations imply that high patient acuity combined with incivility increases risk of fatigue and ultimately enacted incivility. This overextends the supported moderation result, which applied only to the first path.
issues.quote: “Taken together, these results reveal the indirect effect is not conditional upon perceived patient acuity.”

issues.description: The relative importance analysis is interpreted as showing compassion fatigue is a stronger driver of enacted incivility, but predictors are highly correlated and the outcome shares the same measurement occasion with compassion fatigue. Relative importance decompositions under extreme multicollinearity and common-method overlap are unstable and should not be interpreted causally.
issues.quote: “the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions… The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.”

issues.description: All substantive variables are self-reported by the same person using similar Likert-type frequency scales. Temporal separation reduces some immediate consistency bias but does not eliminate stable response tendencies, negative affectivity, social desirability, or percept-percept inflation—especially given the very high correlations among constructs.
issues.quote: “First, our data were collected using self-report questionnaires.”

issues.description: Mean enacted incivility is around the midpoint of a scale from Never to Always, implying nurses reported fairly frequent condescending, derogatory, or dismissive behavior toward patients/families. This is unexpectedly high for a socially undesirable clinical behavior and may indicate sample bias, measurement problems, careless responding, or item ambiguity.
issues.quote: “T4 Enacted Incivility | 2.77 | 1.21”

issues.description: Given open online recruitment, the data-quality checks are limited mainly to demographic consistency and missingness. The manuscript does not report checks for duplicate entries, bots, IP/geolocation anomalies, speeding, straightlining, impossible work patterns, or professional credential verification. This is concerning because 78 participants were already excluded for poor quality.
issues.quote: “Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods…; or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions…”

issues.description: The manuscript asserts that one-week lags are sufficient and comparable to longer lags, but compassion fatigue and enacted incivility may operate on different time scales. No empirical sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification is provided for why exactly one week is appropriate for each path in the serial mediation.
issues.quote: “Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient for observing emergence of such counterproductive behaviors as incivility and that the observed effects will not meaningfully differ from studies featuring longer periods of time between waves…”

issues.subcategory: weekly retrospective windows confound intervening exposures
issues.description: Each wave asks about the past week, but the models do not control for incivility, emotions, or workload occurring during intervening weeks. For example, T3 negative emotions may be driven by T3-week incivility rather than T2 incivility. This weakens temporal interpretation of the lagged paths.
issues.quote: “For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.”

issues.description: Table 1 is titled as including Time 1 controls, but the regression tables mainly show work-hours controls and do not clearly report the role of T1 incivility, T1 negative emotions, T1 compassion fatigue, or T1 enacted incivility. The analytic strategy for controls is therefore unclear and not reproducible.
issues.quote: “Table 1 | Correlation and Descriptive Information for Hypothesized Model with Time 1 Controls”

issues.description: The chi-square statistic is reported without the chi-square symbol and with unclear degrees of freedom formatting. Alternative model fit statistics are not provided despite being invoked. This prevents readers from evaluating the measurement model evidence.
issues.quote: “The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.”

issues.description: Tables contain repeated headers and duplicated notes, and Table 3 has confusing duplicated columns. This impairs transparency and makes it difficult to determine the exact models, coefficients, and sample sizes used.
issues.quote: “Table 3 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  Moderated regression results | Moderated regression results | Moderated regression results…”

issues.subcategory: ambiguity of same versus different patients
issues.description: The theory alternates between reciprocal incivility, spillover to future customers, and chronic hassle exposure, but the design does not identify whether the patients/families at later waves are the same people, different people, or a mix. This limits interpretation of “incivility begets incivility” as reciprocity, displacement, or generalized spillover.
issues.quote: “depending on the nature of the shift and patient care needs, the length of any one patient-nurse relationship is likely brief.”

issues.description: The manuscript argues that customer interactions are fleeting and therefore retaliation is less relevant, but also acknowledges that patients may continue across waves. Because relationship continuity and retaliatory motives were not measured, the proposed stressor-emotion mechanism cannot be distinguished from direct retaliation or repeated conflict with the same patient/family.
issues.quote: “another limitation to the longitudinal design of this study is the chance that an employee may continue an uncivil relationship with certain patients across various time points (i.e., via retribution pathways).”

issues.description: The authors replaced “customer” with “patient” or “patient family members/friends” across scales. Such wording changes can alter item meaning, especially in clinical contexts. The manuscript provides limited evidence that the adapted measures retain validity and measurement equivalence.
issues.quote: “Because of the healthcare sample, the word ‘customer’ was replaced with ‘patient’ or ‘patient or patient family members/friends’ for any scales that asked about customer interactions.”

issues.description: The manuscript states that it examines coworker incivility in the compassion fatigue section, although the study is about patient/customer incivility. This suggests conceptual imprecision and may confuse the construct being tested.
issues.quote: “Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.”

issues.description: The manuscript uses “patient incivility,” “customer incivility,” “experienced patient incivility,” and “customer incivility” interchangeably, including in tables. Inconsistent terminology makes it harder to track constructs and may obscure whether patients, family members, or customers generally are the intended referent.
issues.quote: “T1 Customer Incivility”

issues.description: Race and ethnicity are reported as if mutually exclusive categories, with Hispanic/Latino listed alongside racial categories. This can misclassify respondents and limits interpretability of sample composition.
issues.quote: “74.55% of the respondents self-identified as White, 15.45% self-identified as Hispanic or Latino, 5.76% self-identified as Black, and 4.85% self-identified as Asian.”

issues.description: The study uses a mostly female nursing sample in high-stakes settings, but conclusions and title refer broadly to customers and service employees. Healthcare-specific constraints and power dynamics may not generalize to other service contexts.
issues.quote: “This adds to the generalizability of prior customer incivility research to further support that experiencing incivility from customers – even when the customers are patients…”

issues.description: The outcomes are bounded ordinal frequency scales and likely skewed, especially enacted incivility. The manuscript does not report distributions, floor/ceiling effects, residual diagnostics, or robust/nonlinear modeling for the regression models. Violations could affect estimates and inference.
issues.quote: “Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always).”

issues.subcategory: ordinal CFA but unclear regression treatment
issues.description: The CFA uses WLSMV appropriate for ordinal items, but the mediation and moderation regressions appear to use manifest scale scores as continuous variables. The manuscript does not justify this change in measurement treatment or report whether results are robust to ordinal/latent modeling.
issues.quote: “We applied procedures recommended by Nye and Drasgow (2011) to model the data at the item-level using WLSMV in MPlus 8.0.”

issues.subcategory: no model fit for structural models
issues.description: Only the CFA fit is reported. The manuscript does not report fit indices for the longitudinal mediation or moderated mediation models, making it difficult to evaluate whether the hypothesized structural model adequately fits the data.
issues.quote: “Before evaluating our hypotheses, we investigated the discriminant validity of our measures by employing a series of confirmatory factor analyses.”

issues.description: The moderation analysis does not state whether predictors were centered, standardized, or left in raw units before computing the interaction. This affects interpretability of main effects, simple slopes, and the size of the interaction coefficient.
issues.quote: “Results revealed that the Time 2 experienced incivility × Time 2 perceived patient acuity interaction term was significant (B = .34, SE = .12, p < .01).”

issues.description: The manuscript does not report how many participants came from each recruitment source, hospital, unit, state, or online forum. Without this information, the sample cannot be characterized, replicated, or assessed for clustering and selection effects.
issues.quote: “Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies.”
